explore_lens_curvature_note: Spacetime grid, lensed by the geodesics — an analogy for curvature, not a literal surface.
explore_lens_story_cosmic_web_body: The largest pattern there is: galaxies are not scattered at random but strung along filaments and sheets around near-empty voids, a structure that looks like foam or a web of glowing threads. This shell is a heavily schematic model — a diagram of the idea, not a survey — showing a handful of the great walls, superclusters, and voids of the nearby universe. It is the fossil of tiny ripples in the infant cosmos, grown over billions of years by gravity.
explore_lens_story_laniakea_body: 'Immense heaven' in Hawaiian — the supercluster defined in 2014 not by where galaxies sit but by where they flow. Some 160 megaparsecs (500 million light-years) across, containing about 100,000 galaxies, Laniakea is the basin of attraction our Virgo Supercluster drains into, toward the Great Attractor. And Laniakea, with its neighbours, is part of a broader flow toward something larger still: the Shapley Concentration.
explore_lens_story_lg_body: The Milky Way, Andromeda, the Triangulum galaxy and dozens of smaller companions, bound by gravity across some 10 million light-years. Andromeda and the Milky Way are drifting toward each other and may merge a few billion years from now — recent simulations put it closer to a coin-flip.
explore_lens_story_ls_body: The galaxy groups just beyond the Local Group lie in a thin, nearly flat layer — the Local Sheet — moving together within the wider Local Volume. It is a first glimpse of the cosmic web's geometry: galaxies are not scattered at random but tend to lie along sheets and filaments.
explore_lens_story_mw_body: A barred spiral of a few hundred billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The overlays show what the eye can't: the nearly flat rotation curve, the dark-matter halo it implies, and the stellar populations that record how the disc, bulge and halo were built.
explore_lens_story_nb_body: The Sun's nearest stars, placed at their true distances and colours. The teaching layers trace the constellation figures, pick out the deep-sky objects, sort the stars on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, and ripple light-travel time outward from the Sun.
explore_lens_story_virgo_body: Our home supercluster — a hundred or more galaxy groups and clusters spread across some 33 megaparsecs (about 110 million light-years, and larger by some definitions), dominated by the Virgo Cluster. It was long thought the largest structure we belong to; Laniakea later revealed it to be one lobe of something far bigger.

explore_lens_time_note: Closer to the horizon, time runs slower relative to a far-away clock — the factor is √(1 − rₛ/r). Shown for a non-spinning black hole; real spinning ones shift the photon sphere and orbits inward.

fly_fd_phase_approach_body: Closing on the destination. V∞ is the excess speed at infinity — the speed the spacecraft would have if the planet's gravity weren't there. It sets the minimum braking ∆v before any orbit insertion.
fly_fd_phase_arrival_body: The arrival burn slows the vehicle from its hyperbolic V∞ down below the destination's escape velocity, capturing it into a closed orbit. Miss this burn and the spacecraft flies past forever.
fly_fd_phase_cruise_body: Coasting along a Hohmann transfer — the most fuel-efficient ellipse that touches both planets' orbits. The Sun is the only force; vis-viva gives the speed at every point. No fuel burning, no engine — coast time is free.
fly_fd_phase_departure_body: C3 is the squared launch energy a vehicle has after escaping Earth. A positive C3 means the spacecraft is leaving Earth's gravity well; the higher the number, the faster the cruise.
fly_fd_phase_injection_body: The injection burn (TLI for the Moon, TMI for Mars) is the largest single ∆v of the trip. After it, the engine is off and the vehicle coasts on a Keplerian arc all the way to the destination.
fly_fd_phase_injection_title: Trans-X injection · committing to the arc
fly_fd_phase_separation_body: After the injection burn, the spacecraft separates from the upper stage, deploys its solar panels and antennas, and begins the long coast. The first trajectory-correction maneuver verifies the arc.

lab_goal_gtm_transfer: Mars rides a bigger, slower orbit around the Sun. The same Hohmann trick as the Moon, one scale up: one burn to swing out to Mars’s orbit, coast a long arc across the solar system, one burn to arrive.
lab_goal_gtm_verdict: Do you have the Δv to make the crossing? This is the Δv from Earth's orbit around the Sun — on top of everything it took to leave Earth in the first place.
lab_goal_gtm_window: You can't leave whenever you like — Earth and Mars must be lined up so Mars is actually there when your arc reaches its orbit. That alignment only comes around about every 26 months.
lab_goal_lar_force: It all starts with one law: a force changes a mass's motion. Push harder, or make it lighter, and it speeds up faster.
lab_goal_lar_launch_site: Where on Earth you launch from is a free head start: the planet's spin already carries the pad eastward — fastest at the equator, nothing at the poles. That is why Ariane flies from Kourou, and why companies tow platforms out to sea.
lab_goal_lar_momentum: A rocket moves by throwing mass out the back. The momentum it gives the exhaust is the momentum it gains going forward.
lab_goal_lar_required: How much Δv does orbit actually demand? Not a magic number — it is the orbital speed you must reach (set by this world’s gravity and size) plus the losses fighting up through gravity and air. On Earth about 9.4 km/s; a smaller, airless world asks far less.
lab_goal_lar_tsiolkovsky: Burning propellant builds up speed. The rocket equation ties how fast the exhaust leaves and how much propellant you carry to the delta-v you gain.
lab_goal_lar_twr: For liftoff, thrust has to beat weight. If the thrust-to-weight ratio is below one, the rocket never leaves the pad.
lab_goal_lar_verdict: Now add it up: your rocket's Δv plus the free head-start from your launch site, against what orbit demands. A better site buys margin — or lets you fly a smaller rocket for the same job.
lab_goal_lar_weight: Gravity pulls on every mass with a force we call weight. To leave the ground, something has to push back harder than this.
lab_goal_lom_airbags: The cheap way the early rovers landed: bounce down inside inflated airbags. But they only survive so hard a hit — about 25 m/s. Your parachute leaves you faster than that, so airbags alone will not do it either; Pathfinder fired small retros first to slow down before it bounced.
lab_goal_lom_parachute: So you deploy the biggest parachute the airflow will allow. It helps — but on Mars even a huge chute only gets you down to tens of metres per second. Still not survivable.
lab_goal_lom_retro: So you add a retro-booster: it fires downward to kill the speed the parachute could not. The two methods together — free drag plus paid thrust — are how you actually land. On the airless Moon the parachute does nothing and the booster does it all; on Earth the chute alone is enough. Same physics, different world.
lab_goal_lom_terminal: Mars has air — but barely. A capsule falling through it reaches terminal velocity, where drag balances weight. Because the air is roughly one-sixtieth of Earth's, that speed is still hundreds of metres per second.
lab_goal_lom_verdict: Compare your terminal speed to a safe touchdown. On Mars you come up short — the thin air can't finish the job, so you must fire engines the rest of the way. That is why every Mars lander ends under power.
lab_goal_lov_aeroshell: So Venera let go of its parachute at about 47–50 km — deliberately — and fell the last hour on nothing but its flat aeroshell disc. In air this thick, even that lands you at roughly 7 m/s, about the speed of dropping off a garden wall. Drag alone does what Mars needed rockets for.
lab_goal_lov_chute: Open a parachute in Venus's lower atmosphere and you drift down at walking pace — but that gentleness is a trap: the descent would take so long that the heat would kill the lander before the ground does. Watch what the same chute that barely helped on Mars does here.
lab_goal_lov_corridor: On Mars the entry corridor is a knife-edge; here it is a barn door. Air this dense will capture you across a huge band of entry angles — the Venera probes dove in steeply on purpose to shorten the trip through the furnace. Getting captured is not the problem on Venus.
lab_goal_lov_entry: Venus meets you with an atmosphere about ninety times Earth's surface pressure. Hit it directly from interplanetary speed at a steep angle and it stops you almost at once — the deceleration peaks above a hundred g. No crew could ride this; the Venera landers were built like submarines and took it.
lab_goal_lov_verdict: Check the touchdown: the aeroshell-only fall arrives slower than the shock ring can survive. Venus passes with no retro-rockets and no parachute at the surface — the exact inverse of Mars. The real enemy waits after landing: at ~460 °C, the lander has about an hour to live.
lab_goal_ltm_descent: The landing burn pays twice: cancel the orbital speed you are carrying, and hold yourself up against gravity the whole way down. Add them for the descent Δv.
lab_goal_ltm_orbit: You are circling the Moon. To land, first know how fast you are going — orbital speed here is far slower than at Earth, because the Moon pulls so much more gently.
lab_goal_ltm_twr: Landing is a controlled fall. To slow down and hover, your engine must out-push lunar gravity — thrust-to-weight above one, or you simply keep falling.
lab_goal_ltm_verdict: Does your lander carry enough Δv to cancel its orbit and settle softly onto the surface? Come up short and it is a crash, not a landing.
lab_goal_motion_drop: Let go of a mass and gravity does the rest — it speeds up as it falls. How long does it take, and how fast is it at the bottom?
lab_goal_motion_throw: Throw a mass and gravity curves its path. The launch speed and angle set how far it flies before it lands.
lab_goal_rtm_hohmann: The cheapest way to raise your orbit is a stretched ellipse that just touches both: one burn to leave, a half-lap coast, one burn to arrive. Stretch it all the way out to the Moon.
lab_goal_rtm_orbit: Going straight up isn't enough — you'd just fall back. To stay up, go sideways fast enough that the ground curves away as fast as you fall. That speed is the circular orbital velocity.
lab_goal_rtm_verdict: Add the two burns: that is the Δv to reach the Moon FROM low Earth orbit — on top of the ~9.4 km/s it already took just to get to orbit. Does your on-orbit budget cover the transfer?
lab_goal_rtm_visviva: Orbits aren't all circles. Vis-viva gives your speed at any point of any orbit from just two numbers — where you are, and how big the orbit is. It's the tool every transfer is built from.

landing_section_tour_p1: Start at /explore. Spin the solar system. Click any planet to read its orbital elements — semi-major axis, eccentricity, true anomaly. The numbers are live.
landing_section_tour_p2: Find a mission you care about in /missions — Curiosity, Apollo 11, anything from Sputnik onward. Read its FLIGHT tab to see the actual ∆v budget broken down across the five phases of every spaceflight: launch, trans-X injection, cruise, orbit insertion, EDL.
landing_section_tour_p3: When something doesn't make sense — when a number on the HUD or a label on a chart confuses you — every term is linked to /science. The encyclopedia is meant to be read in order or hopped through depending on what you need.
landing_section_tour_p4: /plan and /fly are the deeper end. /plan computes porkchop diagrams for any destination — pick a launch year, see when the windows open. /fly takes a mission and walks you through its trajectory phase by phase. The HUD shows everything in real units.
landing_section_what_p1: Orrery is a browser-based solar system explorer, mission simulator, and encyclopedia. Real orbital mechanics under the hood — Keplerian two-body propagation, Lambert solvers for transfer trajectories, the same equations real flight teams use. No backend. No accounts. Runs offline once it's loaded.
landing_section_what_p2: It's not a flight planner. There's no API to NORAD, no real-time TLE updates, no live launch-window predictions. The numbers are physically correct but stylised; the missions in the catalogue are real but their flight arcs are teaching models, not propagated state vectors.
landing_section_what_p3: Designed for everyone — curious lay people, students, space enthusiasts, mission planners who want a sandbox. Built for the browser so it works on any device with a screen. Open source under MIT. The catalogue covers real missions across the inner solar system plus the Moon and four outer-planet destinations, and a fleet inventory of the spacecraft that flew them.
landing_section_why_p1: The project started during the lead-up to Artemis II. NASA was about to send four humans around the Moon for the first time since 1972, and the public conversation around it was almost entirely uninformed. People didn't know what 'free-return trajectory' meant. They didn't know why Mars launch windows happen every 26 months. They didn't know the rocket equation.
landing_section_why_p2: Orrery is the answer to that. Spaceflight is built on physics that's been understood since Newton. Most of what looks magical is actually visible — you can see the orbits, you can compute the transfer arcs, you can read every formula. The simulator is the front door; the encyclopedia is the textbook; together they're the project.

programs_index_intro: Spaceflight is usually remembered as a string of missions and machines. But nothing here happened on its own — every rocket, every landing, every station was the work of a {program}: a sustained campaign, backed by a nation or a company, reaching for something specific. science_layer_ascent_losses_desc: Running tally of the gravity, drag & steering Δv spent reaching orbit.
science_layer_atmosphere_desc: Translucent shell at the body's effective atmospheric edge — Kármán line on Earth, ~120 km on Mars.
science_layer_axial_tilt_desc: Spin axis + obliquity arc against the orbital plane — the tilt that drives the seasons.
science_layer_centripetal_desc: Inward acceleration that bends the path into an orbit — gravity itself provides it (a = v²/r), so it points the same way as the gravity arrow.
science_layer_climate_desc: Latitude climate bands (tropical → polar) + how much sunlight this world gets vs Earth and whether its air keeps the heat. Sun is life.
science_layer_coast_desc: Where the spacecraft would drift if the engine cut right now.
science_layer_conics_desc: Names the current arc shape (ellipse / hyperbola / etc.) live.
science_layer_constellations_desc: The constellation figures traced over the nearby stars — patterns the eye projects onto stars that lie at wildly different distances. Neighbours on the sky are rarely neighbours in space.
science_layer_dark_matter_halo_desc: The roughly spherical halo of unseen mass around the disc, inferred from the flat rotation curve. It far outweighs the galaxy's visible stars and gas.
science_layer_dead_dynamo_desc: No global field — only fossil crustal magnetism in the southern highlands. With the shield gone, the solar wind stripped most of the air.
science_layer_deep_sky_desc: Nebulae, star clusters, and galaxies beyond the individual stars — the 'faint fuzzies' Messier and the NGC catalogued, each a different kind of object at a different distance.
science_layer_drag_desc: Aerodynamic resistance opposing the rocket's motion.
science_layer_far_side_desc: The hemisphere that never faces Earth — unseen until Luna 3 photographed it in 1959. Heavily cratered, almost no maria.
science_layer_galaxies_desc: Billboard sprites of ~15 neighbouring galaxies (Andromeda, Magellanic Clouds, dwarf spheroidals) on the celestial sphere at correct RA/Dec — sky-overlay only, not true scale.
science_layer_gravity_desc: Force arrows from each body, log-scaled so all are visible.
science_layer_hill_sphere_desc: The boundary where this planet’s gravity dominates over the Sun’s. Stylised radius (real Hill spheres can exceed the planet’s orbit).
science_layer_hover_desc: Live numbers (speed, distance, gravity) when hovering a planet.
science_layer_hr_diagram_desc: Plots the nearby stars by colour (surface temperature) against brightness. Most fall on the main sequence; red giants sit above it and white dwarfs below it, tracing where a star has been in its life.
science_layer_hydrosphere_desc: 71% of the surface is ocean — Earth is the only known world with stable surface liquid water.
science_layer_lagrange_points_desc: L1 + L2 markers along the planet→Sun line. JWST orbits Earth’s L2; SOHO sits at Earth’s L1.
science_layer_light_cones_desc: Concentric shells at fixed look-back times around the Sun. Light travels at a finite speed, so to look farther out is to look further into the past.
science_layer_mag_north_desc: Geographic pole (spin axis) vs magnetic pole — the offset a compass reads as declination.
science_layer_magnetosphere_desc: Stylised magnetic-field shell + dipole axis. Jupiter’s mag-tail extends past Saturn’s orbit in reality.
science_layer_mars_moons_desc: Two captured-asteroid moons. Phobos orbits faster than Mars rotates, so it rises in the west and sets in the east; it will break up into a ring in ~50 Myr.
science_layer_microgravity_desc: Three colour-keyed body axes — zenith / nadir, prograde / retrograde, port / starboard.
science_layer_moons_desc: Major moons + orbit rings around each planet (Galilean at Jupiter, Titan/Enceladus/Iapetus at Saturn, the Moon at Earth, Phobos/Deimos at Mars, Triton at Neptune).
science_layer_ozone_desc: Polar ozone-depletion zones — Antarctic + Arctic — that open seasonally as ClO and BrO catalyse O₃ destruction in the stratosphere.
science_layer_planet_stats_desc: Floating overlay with surface gravity, atmospheric pressure, and rotation period. Visible only at planet focus.
science_layer_polar_caps_desc: Seasonal CO₂ frost over perennial water ice. They grow and shrink as each hemisphere tips toward and away from the Sun.
science_layer_rotation_curve_desc: How orbital speed changes with distance from the galactic centre — it stays nearly flat out to ~15–20 kpc instead of falling away, the classic hint of unseen mass.
science_layer_soi_desc: Translucent rings marking where each body's gravity dominates — an approximation for planning trajectories, not a physical wall.
science_layer_stellar_populations_desc: Sorts the galaxy's stars into the young, metal-rich disc, the old, metal-poor halo, and the central bulge — a fossil record of how the Milky Way assembled.
science_layer_sub_earth_desc: Earth hangs fixed over this spot — the Moon is tidally locked. Libration lets us see 59% of the surface over a month.
science_layer_sub_solar_desc: Marker at the longitude where it’s currently noon — the point directly under the Sun.
science_layer_thrust_desc: Engine force driving the rocket up its body axis.
science_layer_tidal_lock_desc: Marks the Moon's near-side (always-Earth-facing) hemisphere — the result of synchronous rotation.
science_layer_tides_desc: Twin tidal bulges raised by the Moon — one beneath it, one on the far side. Two high tides a day.
science_layer_velocity_desc: Tangent arrows showing instantaneous heliocentric speed.
science_meta_description: In-app encyclopedia of orbital mechanics, transfers, propulsion, mission phases, scales & time, and porkchop reading — every formula and named term Orrery references.
science_panel_earth_body: A 100 km Kármán-line shell separates atmosphere from space; LEO begins another 100 km up. The ozone column at ~30 km blocks the UV-C that would otherwise sterilise the surface — its polar depletion is one of the few global atmospheric measurements visible from orbit.
science_panel_earth_title: Earth · 6371 km radius, our orbital perch
science_panel_mars_body: Mars' atmospheric pressure sits at 0.6 % of Earth's — enough for parachute aerobraking but not aerocapture. The global magnetic dynamo died ~4 Gyr ago; the residual crustal magnetism in the southern highlands is the only fossil record of when it was alive.
science_panel_mars_title: Mars · thin CO₂ shell + a dynamo gone quiet
science_panel_moon_body: Lunar surface gravity is 1/6 g; a vacuum-thin exosphere offers no aerobraking, so every mission has to carry full ∆v for the descent. Apollo's free-return trajectory let the Earth-Moon-Earth figure-8 act as a built-in abort path.

why_aphelion_body: The farthest point of the orbit from the Sun (or parent body). The slowest point — vis-viva: large r → small v. Good place to nudge the orbit cheaply (small ∆v moves the opposite side a lot) but bad for big burns.
why_arrival_inclination_body: The tilt of the captured orbit versus the destination's equator. Polar orbits (90°) see the whole surface every day but cost more ∆v at insertion. Equatorial orbits (0°) are cheap but see only a band.
why_axial_tilt_body: The angle between a body's spin axis and the perpendicular to its orbit. Earth's 23.4° gives us seasons. Uranus's 98° means it rolls along its orbit on its side. The tilt also sets where the sun rises and sets at landing sites — critical for solar-power planning.
why_caveat_reconstructed_body: Public flight records vary by mission. RECONSTRUCTED means we synthesised numbers from secondary sources (trajectory papers, agency press kits, peer-reviewed reanalysis). They're our best honest estimate, not raw telemetry.
why_caveat_sparse_body: Some agencies released only partial flight data. SPARSE flags missions where headline numbers exist but key parameters (like mid-cruise speeds or per-burn ∆v) were never made public.
why_caveat_unknown_body: We haven't yet researched flight data for this mission. The mission is real and historically documented, but the structured numbers used for visualisations aren't sourced yet.
why_dla_body: DLA is the latitude of the spacecraft's outbound velocity vector relative to Earth's equator. It constrains which launch sites can reach the trajectory: a high-latitude DLA needs a high-inclination launch and costs ∆v.
why_dv_required_body: The number adds three pieces: the launch energy needed to escape Earth (C3), the cruise burns to shape the transfer ellipse, and the orbit-insertion burn at arrival (zero for a flyby). Cells in the cheap teal lobe sit near a Hohmann minimum; ridges flag synodic gaps where physics makes you wait or pay.
why_earth_altitude_body: Altitude bands (LEO ≤ 2 000 km, MEO ≤ 35 786, GEO at 35 786, HEO above) trade off ground resolution, coverage, communication latency, and launch cost. Operators pick altitude to match the mission — imaging wants low, GPS wants medium, broadcast wants geosynchronous.
why_earth_inclination_body: Inclination is the orbit's tilt versus Earth's equator. 0° (equatorial) is cheap from low-latitude launch sites; 51.6° (ISS) is the lowest inclination Russian launches reach without flying over populated areas; ~98° (sun-synchronous) keeps the same lighting for imaging. It's a constraint, not a choice.
why_earth_period_body: Period and altitude are locked together by Kepler's third law. LEO satellites complete a lap every ~90 minutes, MEO every ~12 hours, GEO every 24 hours (matching Earth's rotation). The period decides how often the satellite passes a given ground point.
why_eccentricity_body: How squashed the ellipse is. e=0 is a perfect circle; e→1 is a knife-edge ellipse. High eccentricity means big swings in distance and speed between perihelion (close, fast) and aphelion (far, slow) — the orbit feels lopsided.
why_entry_velocity_body: The speed the vehicle hits the destination's atmosphere at, after gravitational pull has accelerated it. Sets the heat-shield design — every km/s extra means dramatically more heating during entry, descent, and landing.
why_eva_time_body: Extravehicular activity (EVA) is the highest-risk, highest-reward portion of a crewed mission. Suit consumables, micrometeoroid exposure, and CO₂ scrubbing limits cap each EVA at about 8 hours. Total EVA time on a mission is the real measure of how much surface science got done.
why_inclination_body: The orbit's tilt versus the reference plane (ecliptic for heliocentric orbits, equator for Earth orbits). High-inclination orbits cost more ∆v to reach but unlock unique geometries — polar imaging, sun-synchronous lighting, north-south coverage.
why_landing_site_body: Landing sites are a tradeoff: equatorial latitudes are cheap and warm but low-information; polar sites preserve volatiles (water ice in permanently shadowed craters) and are scientifically rich but costly. Specific coordinates target a geological feature — a crater rim, an ancient lakebed, a fresh impact site.
why_mass_tli_body: The wet mass right after the trans-X injection burn drives every downstream calculation: cruise ∆v budget, structural loads, even the entry mass for landers. Two missions can have similar payloads but very different masses at TLI depending on staging.
why_mean_velocity_body: The average orbital speed. Closer-in bodies move fast (Mercury averages 47 km/s); outer bodies crawl (Neptune averages 5.4 km/s). Vis-viva ties velocity to position on the ellipse — perihelion is fast, aphelion is slow.
why_module_length_body: Module length is constrained by the rocket's payload fairing — the aerodynamic nose cone that protects the module during launch. Falcon 9's fairing is 13.2 m tall; Long March 5B's is 20 m. Modules longer than the fairing simply can't fly on that rocket.
why_module_mass_body: Mass to LEO is the unforgiving currency of station construction. Every kilogram needs ~9.4 km/s of ∆v to reach orbit; that drives launch-vehicle choice and dictates which modules can fly together. Big modules (Zarya, Tianhe) need heavy-lift; small ones can hitch on cargo flights.
why_orbital_period_body: How long one full lap around the Sun (or parent body) takes. Tied to semi-major axis by Kepler's third law: P² ∝ a³. The further out, the slower; Neptune's year is 165 Earth years.
why_peak_speed_body: The fastest the spacecraft moves in the Sun's frame during cruise — usually right after the trans-X injection burn or near perihelion of the transfer arc. Tells you the kinetic energy budget the vehicle is working with.
why_periapsis_body: The orbit's closest point to the destination after insertion. Low periapsis = closer to the planet (better imaging, more drag) but more atmospheric heating; high periapsis = wider orbit, less heating, more fuel needed to get there.
why_perihelion_body: The closest point of the orbit to the Sun (or whatever the orbit is around). The fastest point — vis-viva: small r → large v. For comets, perihelion is when the show happens; for spacecraft, it's the cheapest place to do an Oberth burn.
why_samples_body: Returned samples can be analysed with mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, isotope dating — instruments that are too big or power-hungry to fly. Apollo brought back 382 kg; Chang'e 5 brought 1.7 kg of younger near-side regolith (Oceanus Procellarum). Each kilogram unlocks decades of follow-up science.
why_semi_major_axis_body: Half the long axis of an elliptical orbit — the single most important orbit parameter. Pins the average distance from the Sun and (via Kepler's third law) the orbital period. If you only know one number about an orbit, you want this one.
why_solar_mass_body: Mass sets gravity, gravity sets every orbit. The Sun is 333,000× Earth's mass and dominates the solar system; that one number, with Kepler's laws, predicts where every planet is at every moment.
why_station_altitude_body: Both stations sit in low Earth orbit, ~400 km up. Below ~330 km atmospheric drag eats orbital energy faster than the visiting cargo ships can re-boost. Above ~500 km the inner Van Allen radiation belt starts to bite, and crewed-vehicle range drops. The 350-450 km band is the sweet spot.
why_station_inclination_body: Inclination is set by the launch site, not designer preference. ISS at 51.6° is the lowest inclination Russian Soyuz launches can reach without dropping spent stages on populated land. Tiangong at 41.5° is reachable from Wenchang in southern China without overflying populated areas. Each choice trades launch ∆v for ground-coverage range.
why_station_period_body: Kepler's third law: at ~400 km the period is locked at about 92 minutes. That's 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets per crew day — the body's circadian rhythm gets hammered, which is why crews live on synthetic 24-hour Mission Time set to UTC.
why_station_sunrises_body: 92-minute orbits × 24 hours = 15.6 laps per day, each crossing the day/night terminator twice. Crews see roughly 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets daily. The cabin uses scheduled lighting that follows UTC so circadian rhythm doesn't desynchronise.
why_surface_time_body: Surface duration is bounded by power (solar charge or RTG), thermal cycling, and crew life-support consumables. Apollo's lunar-day window was about 3 Earth days; Mars rovers ride out years on RTG; static landers usually fail when their batteries drop below freezing.
worlds_hub_intro: The worlds you can stand on — each built from real data, close enough to look around. Drop onto a surface, trace a rover's path, watch the terminator move.
lab_goal_loe_capsule: A bare capsule falling through Earth's thick air keeps accelerating until drag balances its weight — its terminal velocity. For a 2-tonne capsule that's about 46 m/s: survivable in principle, but a bone-jarring hit.
lab_goal_loe_parachute: Open a parachute and you multiply the drag area many times over. The same capsule now settles to roughly 10 m/s — slow enough that a splashdown or a crushable seat can soak up the rest.
lab_goal_loe_verdict: Is 10 m/s soft enough to walk away from? That depends on HOW you land: splashing into the ocean or crushing a seat can absorb about 12 m/s, so on Earth — yes. The dense air did almost all the braking for free, and a forgiving landing medium finishes the job. Remember this number: the identical capsule reaches Mars at ~50 m/s — too fast for any seat or airbag, which is why you will watch it fail — and gets no braking at all on the airless Moon.
lab_conn_lar_why: Why do rockets launch near the equator? Earth's own spin gives you a free head-start, and it's fastest at the equator (it falls off with the cosine of your latitude). Europe flies from Kourou at just 5° north to bank the biggest boost; Baikonur at 46° gives up nearly a third of it. That invisible speed is worth real fuel — and less fuel means a smaller rocket.
lab_conn_lar_hook: Newton's cannonball: picture firing a cannon from a mountaintop, harder and harder. Eventually the ground curves away as fast as the ball drops, and it never lands. That 'falling forever' is exactly what an orbit is — and it's the very next lesson.

lab_f_escverd_err_insufficient: Not enough — even with the assist you stay bound to the Sun.
lab_assume_ignore_planet_well: Heliocentric Δv only — excludes climbing out of the departure planet's gravity
lab_goal_lss_escape: To leave the Sun for good you must reach its escape velocity. At Earth's distance — 1 AU — that is about 42 km/s. Drag the distance outward and watch it fall: escape is easier the further out you already are.
lab_goal_lss_helio: But you do not start from rest. A craft at Earth already circles the Sun at ~29.8 km/s, so the extra heliocentric speed you must gain is only 42 − 29.8 ≈ 12.3 km/s. That is the hyperbolic excess v∞ — how fast you are still moving once the Sun has done its worst.
lab_goal_lss_assist: So you cheat, with a gravity assist. Fly close past a planet and — in the Sun’s frame — its motion changes your speed, by up to twice your approach speed (a full 180° turn is the ceiling; real flybys turn less). And it cuts both ways: pass BEHIND the planet and it flings you forward, pass in FRONT and it slows you down — the same slingshot run backwards, which is how MESSENGER braked into Mercury and how Parker Solar Probe keeps falling toward the Sun. Jupiter, massive and fast, bends the hardest, which is why every outer-system probe flew past it.
lab_goal_lss_verdict: Add it up in Δv from low orbit: a strong stage (~8.5 km/s) lands right on the ~8.7 line — the very biggest launches just clear it alone. A flyby supplies the margin and, more to the point, the extra speed to actually TOUR the outer planets instead of limping past escape. That is why Voyager took the slingshots.
lab_conn_lss_why: Leaving the Sun sits right at the edge of chemical rockets: from low orbit the Oberth effect makes solar escape cost only ~8.7 km/s, so the biggest launches (New Horizons) can just manage it on their own. But to reach the outer planets within a human lifetime — and to visit several in one mission — you need the speed a gravity assist adds. That is why the Grand-Tour probes all slingshot past Jupiter.
lab_conn_lss_hook: The Voyagers caught a once-in-176-year alignment of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — the 'Grand Tour' — letting a single probe slingshot from world to world. Miss that window and it would not come round again until the 22nd century.

lab_goal_lss_oberth: Here is the twist that makes it possible: you do not buy that 12.3 km/s out in deep space. You burn from a low parking orbit, deep in Earth's gravity well where speed is cheap — the Oberth effect. From there the Δv to reach v∞ = 12.3 is only about 8.7 km/s, not 12.3. That is within a strong chemical upper stage — which is exactly how New Horizons launched straight onto a Sun-escaping path.
lab_assume_impulsive_burn: Impulsive burn (all Δv applied instantly at periapsis)
lab_goal_sar_size: Launching asks for a Δv; building asks what that TAKES. The rocket equation, solved for mass, is brutal: to carry a payload you carry propellant, and to carry that propellant you carry structure, which needs yet more propellant. Every extra kilo of payload cascades. Watch the curve climb — and note the wall it runs into.
lab_goal_sar_thrust: That whole stack has to leave the pad, so thrust must beat weight: F = TWR·m₀·g. Liftoff thrust-to-weight sits around 1.2–1.5 — too low and gravity eats your Δv while you crawl upward, too high and you shake the rocket apart.
lab_goal_sar_engines: That thrust comes from engines, and you rarely have one big enough: N = ⌈F ÷ thrust-per-engine⌉. This is why a Falcon 9 clusters nine Merlins, a Saturn V five giant F-1s, an Atlas V a single RD-180 — and why the Soviet N1 needed thirty, more than anyone could control.
lab_goal_sar_stage: Here is the wall from the first rung, named: a single stage caps at v_e·ln(1/ε) — about 8 km/s for a good stage, no matter how much fuel you pour in, because you must haul its empty structure the whole way. Orbit needs ~9.4. So you STAGE: drop the dead tank and the next stage starts fresh.
lab_goal_sar_boosters: The other way to buy thrust is sideways. When a heavy payload leaves the core short of liftoff thrust, you strap on parallel boosters — Ariane 5’s two solids, Atlas V’s up to five, Falcon Heavy’s two side cores. Crank the payload up and watch how many you need.
lab_conn_sar_why: A rocket is almost all fuel: only ~2–4% of the mass on the pad reaches orbit; the rest is propellant and structure you burn and throw away. That is why one payload can produce wildly different rockets — the designer trades engine count, staging and boosters against the exponential. Many small engines (Falcon 9’s nine Merlins) or a few giants (Saturn V’s five F-1s); one core plus solids (Atlas V, Ariane 5) or a stack of cores (Falcon Heavy).
lab_conn_sar_hook: The Soviet N1 Moon rocket needed THIRTY first-stage engines and could not synchronise them — all four launches failed. Sixty years on, SpaceX’s Starship fires THIRTY-THREE Raptors and lands the booster: the same clustering bet the N1 lost, finally won with modern engines and avionics. More small engines, or fewer big ones, has been rocketry’s oldest argument.

lab_goal_loe_entry: Now the hard part. You meet the atmosphere at almost 8 km/s, carrying about 30 megajoules per kilogram — about seven times the energy of the same mass of TNT — and every joule must become heat. The shield’s job is to dump it into the air, not the capsule. Come in too steep and the g-load and heating spike (drag the angle up and watch); too shallow and you skip back off into space. That narrow band is the re-entry corridor.

lab_goal_g8_phase: The Moon makes no light of its own — you are watching sunlight sweep across a sphere. The lit fraction you see is ½(1 + cos α), where α is the Sun–Moon–Earth angle: α = 0 when the Moon sits opposite the Sun (full), 180° when it is between us and the Sun (new). Pick a date and the disc shows the real phase for that night — waxing (filling, sunlit on the right) toward full, then waning back to new over about 29.5 days.
lab_conn_g8_why: Phase is pure geometry: the same half of the Moon is always sunlit; we just see it from a changing angle as the Moon orbits us. Full moon = the Sun behind you lighting the whole near side; new moon = the Sun beyond the Moon, its lit face turned away. It is also why the "dark side of the Moon" is a myth — there is a FAR side, but every part gets about two weeks of day and two of night.
lab_conn_g8_hook: The cycle drives more than the calendar: at full and new moon the Sun, Earth and Moon line up enough to raise the biggest "spring" tides — and, when the alignment is near-exact, an eclipse.
lab_conn_g8_moon: See the Moon’s real surface, lit for tonight’s phase

lab_assume_vacuum_speed: Signal at the speed of light in vacuum
lab_goal_g10_regime: Every satellite starts with one choice: how high? Altitude sets everything else. Circular speed FALLS the higher you go (v = √(µ/r)), and the period GROWS (T = 2π√(r³/µ)): a 550 km Starlink circles the Earth every ~96 minutes, a 20,000 km GPS satellite takes about 12 hours. Low means fast, close and short passes; high means slow, distant and lingering.
lab_goal_g10_geo: Push the altitude until the period matches the planet’s day — 23.93 hours for Earth — and something clever happens: the satellite keeps pace with the ground turning beneath it, hanging over one fixed spot. That is geostationary orbit, about 35,786 km up. It is why a TV dish never has to move and one weather satellite can watch a whole hemisphere.
lab_goal_g10_latency: So why not put everything up there? Distance costs time. lab_goal_fc_window: First: you cannot just leave — you launch when the planets line up. Earth and Jupiter align every ~13 months (the window below); that sets when you can start. This is the ceiling: four ideal flybys, summed. It is deliberately optimistic: real flybys never hit the perfect 180° turn, the vectors do not add as neatly as a sum, and it counts gross speed stolen, not the rising energy each further planet demands.
